FV Link Lab

swmm524-fvlink: finite volume on the conduits you choose, dynamic wave everywhere else · EPA SWMM 5.2.4 in WebAssembly · AI use: see About
Run. Pick a model, list one or more conduits as FV links, and run both engines. Stock EPA SWMM 5.2.4 runs the model without the [FV_LINKS] section; swmm524-fvlink runs it with the section. Everything runs in your browser.

Model

This model does not use DYNWAVE routing, so the engine will reject any FV link (ERROR 116). The null check still works.

FV links and run

FV linkCellsPre-check
Leave Cells blank for the default: cells = max(4, ⌈L / 25 ft⌉), so cells are about 25 ft long.
Both options change only what is written to the .out file, and they change it the same way for both runs.

## null gate inside wasm: stock wasm vs FV wasm, 73 EPA models, no [FV_LINKS]
73 of 73 identical (.out bytes; .rpt bar run stamps). ncdc_format stops with ERROR 317 in both.

## cause check: native clang 18 -O2 (glibc) vs native gcc 13.3 -O2 (glibc), stock
Example1, user5, Example3: clang-native .out == gcc-native .out. Example3: clang-native .out == wasm .out.
So the compiler is not what separates wasm from native on Example1 and user5; the remaining difference is the math library (musl in emscripten, glibc native) or wasm codegen, not isolated function by function.

The full verification record (VERIFICATION.md from the package)
Verification: swmm524-fvlink


Engine under test: EPA SWMM 5.2.4 (tag v5.2.4, commit 7952ca8) with
swmm524-fvlink.patch applied, built with gcc 13.3 on Linux
(-O2 -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=0).


Reference: stock 5.2.4 from the same tag, built with the same flags, in
every comparison.


Every number below comes from a file in results/, or from a re-run
described where the number is quoted. Every results file was regenerated on
the final build (fvlink.c dated 10/17/26) on 2026-10-17, except
sweep_no_node_limit.csv, a 2026-10-13 experiment with the node stability
limit switched off.


Five-minute version


Each comparison runs one .inp on stock and on the patched engine, with
one conduit listed in [FV_LINKS]. Three controls back the comparisons:


    

  • Null effect. With no [FV_LINKS], the patched engine reproduces stock
byte for byte on 72 of EPA's 73 regression models. The 73rd stops with the
same error in both.
    • 

  • Determinism. The same FV run twice gives identical .out bytes.
    • 

  • Rebuild. The patch applied to a fresh clone rebuilds a byte-identical
binary. An OpenMP build run with THREADS 2 writes the same .out as the
serial build on 13 FV models (results/omp_check.txt).
    • 



user2. On EPA's user2 model, flagging the one channel that stock
handles badly removes a flow oscillation. Re-run at a 5-s report step:


    

  • Stock: TW01290 peaks at 1,921 cfs while the channel above it carries
at most 891 cfs and the one below it at most 537 cfs. It sends
165,921 ft³ back upstream over 83 reported steps.
    • 

  • FV: TW01290 peaks at 449 cfs with no reversal.
    • 

  • Volume: net volume through the link agrees to 0.02 %.
    • 

  • Stock's own flow instability index calls its run stable.
    • 



Speed. On a 400-pipe tree whose average dynamic wave step is pinned at
1.14 s by one 10-ft pipe, flagging that pipe runs in 0.19× the wall time
(0.17× in the 2026-10-13 session).
Every conduit peak flow stays within 0.53 % of stock, and every node peak
depth within 0.80 %.

Turns at 1-s resolution, by stats.c's rule: 472 stock, 775 FV. So the FV
series isn't smooth either; its swings are smaller (total variation 84,129
vs 225,965 cfs).


An earlier draft reported a 9.5 % volume loss here. That came from summing a
60-s report series of an oscillating flow, and it disappears at 1-s sampling.


Gross inflow at node 1126. The report's gross inflow there falls from
25.8 to 24.4 Mgal. Stock's figure includes the water that sloshes back and
forth.


Mechanism


Why the stock index is blind. SWMM's flow instability index counts
turns: sign changes of dq, the change in a link's flow from one routing step
to the next, counted when |dq| > 0.001 cfs (stats_updateLinkStats,
stats.c:748-751). It counts turns, not their size. It scales the count as
turns * 100 / (2/3 * (steps - 2)) (stats.c:785-790). A link appears in
the table only when its index exceeds 1.


user2 runs 36 h at a 5-s step, about 25,900 steps, so a link needs roughly
170 turns to appear at all. An oscillation with a period of minutes produces
a few dozen: stock's TW01290 has 45 turns in the 5-s series (which is every
routing step), index 0.26. The FV run scores 3: 449 turns, index 2.60, from
small step-to-step wiggles in its delivered flow (total variation 965 cfs
over the run).


Separately, report_writeMaxFlowTurns prints "All links are stable" when
flowTurns[0].index <= 0, which also hides an unstable link at index 0.
That one is read in source but not reproduced (S5-DW3).


Why FV removes the oscillation. Stock carries one flow per conduit,
derived from the two end heads. A steep channel between two nodes with large
surface areas can slosh. The FV link carries its flow on its own cells and
exchanges volume with its end nodes through face fluxes. A semi-implicit
node head update damps the node-pipe mode, and a node stability limit
(A_node/K) keeps it damped.


Removing that limit brings the oscillation back. Measured in the EPA sweep
with the limit switched off (results/sweep_no_node_limit.csv), the user2
maximum node depth difference rose from 1.31 ft to 7.05 ft. The limit stays.


Why mass closes.


    

  • Each FV link's stored volume changes by exactly what crosses its two end
faces. The largest error measured is 2.7e-12 %.
    • 

  • Those face volumes enter the end node's continuity as booked volumes,
through fvlink_getNodeVolume() called from setNodeDepth(). That holds
wherever stock updates a node from its volume change (not surcharged, or
flooding). A node surcharged under EXTRAN takes its head from the net flow
and dQ/dH instead, so there the booking isn't exact.
    • 

  • The reported link flow is the flow the link delivers. Quality routing's
identity qIn = |q1| + dV/dt (qualrout.c:319) therefore returns exactly
the volume that entered the link.
    • 



The closure identities, by construction and measured. The table builder
buildTable() takes SWMM's xsect_getAofY at 256 depths. Where the area
rises, area is piecewise linear in depth, so width is its exact derivative
and I1 its exact integral. scripts/test_closure.c links the engine's own
fvlink.c and calls buildTable() (results/closure.txt):

How to read the table:


    

  • Derivative columns. These are limited by the 1e-6 finite-difference
step, not by the closure.
    • 

  • Width jump. The largest relative change between neighbouring
segments, read on both sides of every knot. It sits at the invert segment,
where width grows fastest: for the triangle the segment widths run 1:3.
    • 

  • Depths bridged. No built-in shape needed any. The one case among the
37 conduits flagged in the EPA set is transect 179 in user5, where 3 of 256 depths were bridged
(S5-DW4, FVL-11).
    • 



Lake at rest (results/gates.txt):


    

  • Head is 105 ft everywhere, and the outfall is FIXED at 105 ft.
    • 

  • C1: 3-ft circle.
    • 

  • C2: rectangular open channel with a 0.5 ft inlet offset.
    • 

  • C3: 2 barrels of 6-ft circle, surcharged.
    •

With every conduit FV, the lake stays still to round-off. A mixed model
doesn't: the FV links' 1e-12 round-off seeds the dynamic wave links, which
then settle at dynamic wave's own noise floor of about 4e-3 cfs. Stock
reaches the same floor from a 1e-7 ft seed.


Resonator (results/gates.txt). A dead-end manhole (12.566 ft²) on a
surcharged 3-ft FV pipe, 300 ft long, draining to a FIXED outfall. J1 starts
0.05 ft high. The largest deviation in each 30-min window:


4.6e-02 1.0e-02 2.2e-03 4.8e-04 1.1e-04 2.3e-05 7.6e-06 0 0 0 0 0



With the original explicit node coupling (FVL-2), the same model grew to a
±2.1 ft limit cycle.


Heads in both gates come from the .out file, whose single-precision values
resolve about 7.6e-6 ft at 105 ft. A drift or deviation of 0 means none at
that resolution; the last nonzero resonator value, 7.6e-06, is one step.

The review found no fault in the null-effect path, the signs, the
hydrostatic corrections, the node booking, the Picard restart, or repeated
open/close cycles in one process (run under valgrind).


Document check and final-build controls


Two more agents checked drafts of the technical description (the Word
document) against the code and these results. The first found 3 wrong
statements, 12 imprecise ones and 4 unsupported ones; the second found 5
more wrong statements and several imprecise ones. All are corrected in the
document and here. The second exposed FVL-14 (the report's lengthening
ratio for an FV link). The first exposed FVL-13: when the fourth node estimate still asked for a
shorter substep, the substep was cut without being recorded or held to the
floor. Counted with an instrumented build (results/pass_count.txt): 18 of
17,885,456 substeps in the sweep, all in test5, each cut under 2 parts in
1e8.

How to read it:


    

  • Mesh refinement on one link (chain30, 1 to 48 cells). The extra head
at the FV link's upstream node shrinks from 0.41 to 0.13 ft. It is
numerical, not an entrance loss. The likely cause is the half-cell bed
step at each conduit end; OpenSWMM's Chapter 8 (commit 8dd7387) describes
the same artificial step at manholes and the same remedy, more cells
(results/openswmm_check.txt). A second likely cause is the Riemann
solver's dissipation at the node faces, which OpenSWMM's solver code names
and avoids at two-conduit junctions with a pass-through ghost. The split
wasn't measured.
    • 

  • Storage outlet (S1, +0.47 ft). The same interface loss, against a
large storage area.
    • 

  • channel_C2. The peak deltas come from the dry start. At steady state
the FV reach sits at 1.6592 ft against Manning normal depth of 1.6559 ft
(+0.20 %) and carries 60.0001 cfs. The DW reaches sit at 1.6559 ft.
    •

(results/timing_*.txt, final build). Run-to-run noise on this machine is
6-30 %, so per-pair ratios are quoted.

What the test networks contain


EPA swmm-nrtestsuite v2.5.0-dev, 73 models (results/sweep.csv):


    

  • 32 models aren't dynamic wave (31 KINWAVE, 1 STEADY). They test only the
null effect.
    • 

  • 4 dynamic wave models have no conduits.
    • 

  • 37 models ran with one conduit flagged: the conduit with the largest stock
peak flow that the FV validator accepts.
      

    • Size: 3 to 209 nodes, 3 to 276 links.
      • 

    • Flagged shapes: 20 circular, 10 trapezoidal, 4 street, 3 irregular.
      • 

    • Default cell counts: 4 to 40.
      • 

    • Units: 5 SI (CMS) models; the rest US (CFS).
      • 

    • All 37 use EXTRAN surcharge. SLOT is tested only in the synthetic
chains.
      • 

    • Three use LENGTHENING_STEP; stock lengthens the flagged link in one
(user4).
      • 

    

    • 



Synthetic (scripts/gen.py):


    

  • Shapes: circular in single and double barrel, rectangular closed,
rectangular open, and trapezoidal.
    • 

  • Nodes: a functional storage unit, plus FIXED, NORMAL and FREE outfalls.
    • 

  • A 0.5 ft offset.
    • 

  • Two consecutive FV links sharing a junction.
    • 



Review probes (models/review/):


    

  • a gated outfall
    • 

  • a pollutant
    • 

  • a reversed, two-barrel, offset conduit
    • 

  • three pump wet wells
    • 

  • a long link ID
    • 



This set can't tell you about:


    

  • egg, horseshoe, gothic or custom conduits in a running model (they are
covered only by the closure gate)
    • 

  • reactive pollutants
    • 

  • ponding
    • 

  • hot start
    • 

  • control rules acting on an FV link
    • 



The sweep in one paragraph:


    

  • FV link volume balance stays at or below 2.7e-12 % in all 37 runs, with
0 floor hits.
    • 

  • System outflow volume changes by a median absolute 0.014 % (signed
median 0.000 %).
    • 

  • The only model above 0.5 % is extran8a, at +22.7 %. It starts with
InitFlow = 20 cfs in two links, and stock dynamic wave recomputes each
link's volume from its end depths in the first step. In stock the two
links' jumps cancel (−0.98 % continuity). With one of them FV, the other's
jump stands (−7.39 %). The imbalance appears in the first 20-s step and
then stays flat. With the initial flows removed, stock gives −6.87 % and
FV −6.70 % (S5-DW1).
    • 

  • The flagged-link peak changes by a median absolute 0.04 %. Four links moved
more than 5 %:
      

    • user2: −73 % (the oscillation above)
      • 

    • user5: −38 % (oscillation)
      • 

    • gate_control_2: +23 % (a gate-release surge that FV carries with a
sharper front; same volume)
      • 

    • gate_control_3: −13 % (a single 60-s report spike)
      • 

    

    • 

  • The largest worst-instant node difference is test3's 15.6 ft at node 7,
during a near-vertical drawdown from a 49-ft surcharge. The drop happens
about one minute apart in the two runs. Peak depths differ by 0.5 ft, and
the steady states agree.
    • 



WebAssembly build (2026-10-21)


The FV Link Lab app runs both engines in the browser. They are the same
source compiled with Emscripten 3.1.51 (system LLVM 18, Binaryen 116),
-O2, single-file glue, run in a Web Worker with a fresh module per run.
Each was run against its native build on every test, gate and probe model
(67 runs) and on all 73 EPA models (results/wasm_check.txt):

  • Inside WebAssembly the null effect holds exactly: the stock and FV
engines write identical bytes on all 73 EPA models.
    • 

  • The report-only differences are the last digit of a 1e-13 % FV volume
balance and the minute at which a flat peak is reported.
    • 

  • The largest .out difference is 16.2 cfs in a 1,962-cfs peak (0.83 %),
in stock dynamic wave on user5. The largest relative one is 0.44 cfs in a
29.8-cfs peak (1.5 %), on review/rev_fvall.inp with every conduit FV.
    • 

  • A native clang 18 build matches the native gcc build on Example1, user5
and Example3, so the compiler is not the cause. The difference follows
the math library (musl in the WebAssembly build, glibc natively). That was
found by elimination, not function by function.
    • 

  • The app itself was tested headless in Chromium (results/app_browser_test.txt):
each of its 9 samples was run through the page's own engines, and the
inputs the page built were run through the native engines. All 18 .out
files are byte-identical; 3 FV reports differ in the 1e-13 % volume
balance digit or a flat peak's time. The page's tree runs reproduce the
tested runs/tree_dw.out and runs/tree_fv.out exactly, and its null
check on the tree is byte-identical.
    • 



What this does not show


    

  • No observed data. Stock dynamic wave is a reference, not the truth.
    • 

  • The extra head at FV link ends is numerical and shrinks with refinement.
It isn't calibrated entrance-loss physics.
    • 

  • "Exact" mass means exact for the FV link and its booking into nodes, except
at a node surcharged under EXTRAN. Whole-model continuity is still dynamic
wave's.
    • 

  • A mixed model at rest sits at dynamic wave's noise floor, not at zero.
    • 

  • Not tested: reactive water quality, ponding, hot start continuity, or
control rules acting on an FV link.
    • 

  • Pumps or dummy conduits drawing from an FV end node are rejected, not
supported.
    • 

  • Native Linux (gcc 13.3, serial and OpenMP) and the WebAssembly build
above. No Windows or MSVC.
    • 

  • No comparison against OpenSWMM's own FV engine.
    • 



Reproduction


git clone --branch v5.2.4 https://github.com/USEPA/Stormwater-Management-Model.git stock
cp -r stock patched && (cd patched && git apply ../swmm524-fvlink.patch)
# build both: gcc -O2 -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=0 -Isrc/solver -Isrc/solver/include src/solver/*.c src/run/*.c -lm
git clone --branch v2.5.0-dev https://github.com/USEPA/swmm-nrtestsuite.git nrtest
scripts/null_gate.sh $STOCK $FV nrtest work/null            > results/null_gate.txt
python3 scripts/suite.py $STOCK $FV models runs results      # results/suite.csv
python3 scripts/sweep.py $STOCK $FV nrtest work/sweep results/sweep.csv
python3 scripts/gates.py $STOCK $FV models runs/gates results/gates.txt
node out-diff.js runs/tree_dw.out runs/tree_fv.out          # results/outdiff_tree.txt
node interleave-timing.js -n 7 --a "$STOCK models/tree_dw.inp a.rpt a.out" --b "$FV models/tree_fv.inp b.rpt b.out"
python3 scripts/oscillation.py $STOCK $FV nrtest/public/user work/osc results/oscillation.txt
scripts/asan_runs.sh $FV_ASAN . runs/asan_final > results/asan.txt   # gcc -O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined
scripts/omp_check.sh $FV $FV_OMP . runs/omp > results/omp_check.txt  # gcc -O2 -fopenmp



Paths given to the scripts must be absolute, because each run starts in the
model's own folder.


Notes:


    

  • out-diff.js and interleave-timing.js are the corinne-testing scripts.
    • 

  • The closure gate builds from the patched src/solver directory:
gcc ... test_closure.c $(ls *.c | grep -v fvlink.c) -lm.
    • 

  • scripts/oscillation.py makes the user2 (5-s) and user5 (1-s)
re-runs itself.
    • 

  • The patch applied to a fresh clone rebuilt a binary byte-identical to the
tested one.
    • 











Defects. Fourteen bugs in this branch, all found and fixed before delivery, and four behaviours of stock SWMM 5.2.4 seen during verification. Each FVL entry shows the code as it stood when the bug was live.
There are two kinds of entry. The FVL- entries are bugs in this branch, all
found and fixed before delivery; they are kept because each one is a trap
for anyone porting the scheme. The S5- entries are stock EPA SWMM 5.2.4
behaviour seen during verification.


Each FVL- entry shows the code as it stood when the bug was live.


Claude found FVL-1 to FVL-5, FVL-11 and FVL-12. FVL-6 to FVL-10 came from an
independent review agent that had not seen the work being built; its probe
models are in models/review/. FVL-13 and FVL-14 came from two more agents
that checked drafts of the technical description against the code.




FVL-1  A still-water ghost choked flow out of the FV link
Engine / version:   swmm524-fvlink, first draft
Where:              src/solver/fvlink.c  solveSystem(), the end-face states
What:               The node ghost had zero velocity, so water leaving the pipe
                    hit a still pool and backed up. The ghost now takes the
                    adjacent cell's velocity; the node supplies only the head.
Reproduce:          gen.chain(qpeak=30, fv=["C4"]): J4 max depth 8.83 ft
                    (stock 1.73 ft); fixed build 1.92 ft
Detected by:        consistency with stock dynamic wave (node depth summary)
Blast radius:       every FV link end
Status:             fixed (uL = velOf(f, f->a[0], f->q[0]); uR likewise).
                    OpenSWMM's ExplicitFvSolver.cpp makes the same choice.



The code as it was:


                    zR = f->z2;
                    etaR = NdH[f->n2];
                    hR = MAX(0.0, etaR - zR);
                    uR = 0.0;



FVL-2  Explicit node coupling pumped a manhole-pipe oscillation
Engine / version:   swmm524-fvlink, second draft
Where:              src/solver/fvlink.c  solveSystem()
What:               The node head at the start of a substep fixed the face
                    fluxes, and those fluxes then advanced the node. That is
                    forward Euler on an oscillator, so energy grew. Fixed with a
                    backward-Euler head estimate per substep, using the end
                    faces' conductance sqrt(g*A*T), and then re-solving those
                    faces at that head.
Reproduce:          models/gates/resonator.inp: a 0.05 ft disturbance grew to a
                    +/-2.1 ft limit cycle. Fixed build: falls ~4.6x per 30 min.
                    In models/gates/lake_C1.inp the mode grew from round-off to
                    1.5 cfs within the 2-h run.
Detected by:        lake-at-rest gate (Corinne test 2). Continuity could not
                    see it, because mass was exact the whole time.
Blast radius:       any FV link with a dead-end or small-area end node
Status:             fixed



The code as it was:


        for (i = 0; i < NNodes; i++)
        {
            n = NodeList[i];
            NdH[n] = nodeHead(n, t, dt);
...
            NdV[f->n1] -= f->fm[0] * f->barrels * dts;
            NdV[f->n2] += f->fm[nc] * f->barrels * dts;

FVL-8  Water quality routing blew up on FV links
Engine / version:   swmm524-fvlink, before review
Where:              src/solver/fvlink.c  setLinkResults()
What:               Quality routing treats a conduit as one flow plus a change

The same review raised two risks, both closed:


    

  • End faces sized on stale speeds. The substep was sized on wave speeds
measured before the end faces were re-solved at the new node heads. The
step is now re-checked against the re-solved faces, for up to four node
estimates (FVL-13 covers the case where the fourth still asks for less).
    • 

  • Silent floor. The 0.001 s floor silently overrode the stability limit.
The report now counts every such substep as a Floor Hit.
    • 



FVL-11  A flat stretch in SWMM's area table meant infinite wave speed
Engine / version:   swmm524-fvlink, found after the review fixes
Where:              src/solver/fvlink.c  geometry table (now buildTable())
What:               Where SWMM's area did not rise with depth, the table forced
                    a 1e-12*aFull step. That gave a near-zero width and a wave
                    speed c = sqrt(gA/W) of tens of thousands of ft/s, which
                    pinned the substep at the floor. The table now keeps SWMM's
                    area at each depth where it reaches a new maximum and joins
                    those depths with straight lines.
Reproduce:          EPA user5 with LIB_9 (transect 179) FV: minimum width
                    3.7e-8 ft at 0.234 ft depth, smax 40,930 ft/s, 69,031
                    substeps forced to the 0.001 s floor. Fixed build: 3 of 256
                    depths bridged, 0 floor hits.
Detected by:        the Floor Hits column added for the FVL-10 review risk
Blast radius:       FV links on irregular or street transects whose width
                    jumps within the first 4 % of depth
Status:             fixed

        a = xsect_getAofY(x, y);
        if ( a <= f->tA[i-1] ) a = f->tA[i-1] + 1.0e-12 * x->aFull;

About. What this page is, where every part of it came from, and how AI was used to make it.




What this is


FV Link Lab runs two real SWMM engines in your browser. One is stock EPA SWMM 5.2.4. The other is swmm524-fvlink, the same code with a new input section, [FV_LINKS]: the conduits you list there are solved by an explicit finite-volume scheme on their own cells, and every other link and node stays stock dynamic wave. The two meet at the nodes they share.


The question behind it was whether one link could be finite volume while the rest of the model stays dynamic wave. OpenSWMM's finite-volume routing switches the whole model; this branch does it per link, on 5.2.4.


Results are in the model's own units. The samples are US customary (cfs, ft). Your files never leave the browser.


Deploying
Drag the folder that holds index.html and swmm524-fvlink-one-pipe-its-own-clock.docx onto Netlify, or run netlify deploy --dir=. --prod in it. Nothing else is needed: the engines are inside the page, single-threaded, so no special headers are required.


What the page stores
Your theme choice and whether you have seen the welcome note, in this browser's local storage. The Make a GIF button loads html2canvas 1.4.1 and gif.js 0.2.0 from cdnjs; nothing else is fetched.


Provenance




Base engineEPA SWMM 5.2.4, tag v5.2.4, commit 7952ca8


Patchswmm524-fvlink.patch: fvlink.c (new, 1,403 lines, dated 10/17/26) and hooks in 11 existing files


Browser buildEmscripten 3.1.51 with system LLVM 18 and Binaryen 116; -O2 -sSINGLE_FILE=1 -sMODULARIZE=1 -sENVIRONMENT=web,worker -sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1 -sSTACK_SIZE=2MB; built 2026-10-21


Engine hashesstock glue sha256 249d5b3853ad82c5…
FV glue sha256 69996b70fedf1e5e…


How a run worksA Web Worker per run, a fresh module per run, the step loop of swmm_run() (open, start, step until done, end, close)


SamplesThe branch's synthetic test networks (scripts/gen.py) and EPA's user2 from swmm-nrtestsuite v2.5.0-dev (report step changed to 30 s, marked in the file)


FiguresDrawn from the branch's results/ files and run outputs; diagrams and the two illustrations are labeled


AI useSee below






AI use


This app, the swmm524-fvlink branch it runs, its tests and its documents were made with Claude, Anthropic's AI model, in Claude Code sessions from October 13 to 21, 2026, under the direction of Robert (Bob) Dickinson. He asked for finite volume on chosen links with dynamic wave on the rest, for the technical description and the essays, and for this app; responsibility for the work is his.


What Claude did. It read the EPA SWMM 5.2.4 and OpenSWMM source, designed the method and chose its parameters, wrote fvlink.c and the hooks, the test networks and scripts, ran every test and fixed the defects in the register. For this app it compiled both engines to WebAssembly, wrote the page (its .inp, .rpt and .out parsers, the network view, the charts, the worker and the recorder), drew every figure from the results files, and wrote all the text, including the Doc tab and its Word version. A second Claude agent reviewed the code without the build history, and two more checked drafts of the technical description against the code.


How it was checked. Mechanically: byte comparison with stock on EPA's 73 regression models, rebuilds from the patch, analytic answers, mass balances, interleaved timing, sanitizer runs, the WebAssembly-against-native census, and a headless Chromium test that runs this page's own engines and compares their files with the native ones. Not yet checked by a person: fvlink.c line by line, a run on a project model, the design choices listed in the package README, and this page's parsers beyond the automated tests.

One Pipe, Its Own Clock
How swmm524-fvlink solves the conduits you choose by finite volume while dynamic wave runs the rest of the model, what that buys, and what it costs
The Doc tab of the FV Link Lab, for Robert Dickinson's swmm524-fvlink branch of EPA SWMM 5.2.4. October 2026.
Download the .docxThe same essay as a Word file. On the Netlify site it sits next to this page; if you opened this file on its own, it is in the swmm524-fvlink package zip.
Contents
  1. The job
  2. What it is
  3. Why one pipe sets the clock
  4. Cutting the pipe into cells
  5. The handshake at the nodes
  6. Follow the data
  7. Checking the work
  8. What this does not show
  9. How to use it
  10. AI use
  11. References
1. The job
Here is the job. You have a sewer model with four hundred pipes. Three hundred and ninety-nine of them are ordinary 300-ft pipes: thirty-nine lengths of 6-ft trunk and 360 laterals of 1.5-ft pipe that feed it. The four hundredth, CT21, is a piece of the 6-ft trunk only ten feet long. Every real network has a few of these, short connectors between two structures that sit close together. This one is in a synthetic test tree built for the purpose, so we know exactly what is in it.
SWMM's dynamic wave solver picks one time step for the whole network, and it picks the step to suit the most demanding conduit. CT21 is the most demanding by a factor of nearly ten. So the model runs at an average step of 1.14 seconds, and all four hundred pipes are computed at that step because one of them needs it. You are paying for that ten-foot pipe four hundred times over.
The second example is worse, because it is quiet about it. EPA's regression model user2 has an irregular channel, TW01290, 544 ft long and falling 8.1 ft. Run it in stock SWMM 5.2.4 and look at the flow every five seconds. The channel peaks at 1,921 cfs while the channel feeding it never carries more than 891 cfs and the channel it feeds never more than 537. Between 12.53 and 12.88 hours it runs backwards 83 times. The report's instability table says All links are stable.
The question that started this was short: in SWMM6, can one link be finite volume and the rest dynamic wave? OpenSWMM's finite-volume routing is a switch for the whole model. This branch is the per-link version, built on EPA SWMM 5.2.4. You list a conduit, and that conduit, and only that conduit, is solved by finite volume on its own mesh of cells. Everything else is stock dynamic wave (Figure 1).
That last sentence is the real job. A new solver that changes everything a little is easy to build and impossible to trust. One that changes nothing until you ask, and then changes only what you asked for, can be checked. Most of what follows is about how it was checked.
2. What it is
swmm524-fvlink is EPA SWMM 5.2.4 with one new source file, fvlink.c (1,403 lines), and short hooks in eleven existing files. It adds an input section, [FV_LINKS], that names conduits and optionally how many cells to cut each into. During a dynamic wave run those conduits are marched by an explicit Godunov-type finite-volume scheme with many small substeps inside each routing step, and their end nodes exchange water with them through exactly booked face volumes. With no [FV_LINKS] section, none of the new code runs and the engine writes the same output, byte for byte, as stock 5.2.4. This app runs both engines, stock and patched, compiled to WebAssembly, in your browser, so you can try it on your own model and see the difference for yourself.
3. Why one pipe sets the clock
Start with what dynamic wave carries. For each conduit it keeps one flow. For each node it keeps one head. Every routing step it solves the momentum equation for each conduit's flow from the two heads at its ends, then updates each node's head from the flows in and out, and repeats that pair of updates (SWMM calls the repeats trials, up to eight of them) until the heads stop moving by more than the head tolerance, 0.005 ft in the tree. That is three numbers for a pipe: two heads and a flow. For a 300-ft pipe carrying a slow flood wave, three numbers are plenty.
The step size comes from the Courant condition. Courant, Friedrichs and Lewy wrote it down in 1928, and every explicit calculation of waves has lived under it since. A disturbance travels along a conduit at the water's velocity plus the wave celerity, c = √(g·A/T), where A is the flow area and T the top width. If the step is long enough for the disturbance to cross the whole conduit, the calculation is no longer following the wave, and it goes wrong. SWMM's variable step takes the model's factor (0.75 in the tree) times L/(v + c) for every conduit that is neither empty, nor full, nor nearly still, and uses the smallest.
Now look at the tree with that rule (Figure 2). Of the four hundred conduits, every one but CT21 allows five seconds or more at its tightest moment. CT21 allows half a second. The network takes the half second.
SWMM's own report shows what that does (Figure 3). With CT21 in the model as ordinary dynamic wave, almost every step falls in the shortest bins and the average is 1.14 s. Hand CT21 to the finite-volume solver and the average goes to 9.89 s. The same tree with the short pipe simply removed averages 9.87 s. In other words, the rest of the network runs as if the short pipe were not there, while the short pipe is still there, at its true length, carrying its flow.
SWMM has an older answer to this, the LENGTHENING_STEP option. It makes short conduits longer, and adjusts their roughness, until they stop setting the step. That works, and engineers have used it for decades, but it changes the pipe. The finite-volume link keeps the pipe and pays for its short length with its own small substeps, inside the link, where nobody else has to take them. Nothing here is free. What it buys is that the small step is taken only where it is needed.
4. Cutting the pipe into cells
The finite-volume link does not carry one flow. It cuts the conduit into cells, about 25 ft each by default and never fewer than four, and carries two numbers in every cell: the area of water, A, and the flow, Q, per barrel (Figure 4). CT21 gets four cells of 2.5 ft. A 300-ft pipe gets twelve. You can give any link the count you want.
Between every pair of cells there is a face, and the whole method is a ledger kept at the faces. In one substep, whatever water crosses a face leaves the cell on one side and enters the cell on the other. A cell's area changes by what came in minus what went out, divided by its length. Add that up along the pipe and every interior face cancels, because each one was counted once as a loss and once as a gain. Only the two end faces are left (Figure 5). That is why the link's volume balance closes to round-off: the stored water changes by exactly what crossed the ends, by construction, not by luck. Measured over 37 EPA models and 14 synthetic cases, the largest volume balance error in any FV link was 2.7e-12 %.
What crosses each face is decided the way Godunov decided it in 1959: treat the two states on either side as a small dam break and ask what water would flow through the face. Solving each dam break exactly is expensive, so the face uses the HLL approximation of Harten, Lax and van Leer (1983). It needs only the fastest waves moving left and right out of the face, and those come from Davis's 1988 estimates, with special cases for a dry bed on either side. The result is a flux that is upwind when the flow is fast and centered when it is slow, without anyone having to say which is which.
There are four places where a careless scheme goes wrong in a sewer, and each one cost a decision.
  • Still water must stay still. A bed that slopes, or a pipe that enters a manhole above its floor, puts a step in the bottom. A naive scheme sees the pressure difference across the step and makes a current out of nothing. The faces here use the hydrostatic reconstruction of Audusse and his colleagues (2004), which balances the pressure against the bed exactly. The test is a lake at rest, and it comes later.
  • A full pipe must still carry a wave. When a closed pipe fills, the free surface disappears and the open-channel equations stop being well posed. The link adds Preissmann's slot (1961), an imaginary narrow slot in the crown whose width makes the pressure wave travel at 100 ft/s, capped at 5 % of the pipe's maximum width (Figure 6). The price is the substep: a full pipe subcycles at 100 ft/s whatever its length.
  • Friction must not blow up when the pipe runs shallow. Manning friction is applied semi-implicitly, and on the real section area only. The slot holds water, but it does not convey any. A first version let the slot area count as conveyance (FVL-4).
  • No cell may be drained below empty. Each face's outflow is limited by what the cell or node it drains from actually holds, so a dry cell stays dry instead of going negative.
The geometry comes from SWMM itself. When the link starts, it asks SWMM's own xsect_getAofY for the area at 256 depths and joins them with straight lines. That makes the top width the exact derivative of that table and the pressure moment its exact integral, so depth from area is an exact inverse. On eleven of SWMM's built-in shapes the round trip, depth to area and back, closes to 3.4e-14 ft or better. The FV link sees the same pipe dynamic wave sees, not a lookalike.
Every substep is held to half of what the Courant condition allows inside the link: the fastest signal in any cell may cross at most half a cell. CT21's shortest substep was 0.0878 s, and it took about 105 of them per routing step (the count includes every trial of every step). That is the cost of the short pipe, paid in one place.
5. The handshake at the nodes
The hard part of a hybrid is never either half. It is the joint. At each end of the FV link sits a node that dynamic wave also owns, with other conduits attached that are still dynamic wave. The two methods have to agree on how much water is in that node and how high it stands, every substep, or the model leaks.
The ghost
Each end face needs a state on its outer side, and there is no cell there. So the link builds a ghost: a state whose water surface is the node's head and whose velocity is the velocity of the adjacent cell. Head given, velocity extrapolated. The first draft gave the ghost zero velocity, which sounds harmless and is not. Water leaving the pipe ran into a still pool, backed up, and the node upstream of the FV link in the 30 cfs test chain reached 8.83 ft against stock's 1.73 ft (FVL-1). This is the line that did it:
fvlink.c, first draft, the downstream ghost (FVL-1)
                    zR = f->z2;
                    etaR = NdH[f->n2];
                    hR = MAX(0.0, etaR - zR);
                    uR = 0.0;
With the ghost taking the cell's velocity, the same node peaks at 1.92 ft. OpenSWMM's ExplicitFvSolver.cpp makes the same choice.
Who keeps the books for the node
During the subcycle, an end node can be in one of two modes. A junction, storage unit or divider is LOCAL: it keeps its own continuity, substep by substep, with the FV face flows and the dynamic wave flows from its other links. An outfall is PRESCRIBED: its head is whatever dynamic wave says it is, and so is the head of a node surcharged under EXTRAN, whose head stock SWMM computes from the net flow rather than from a volume. A flap-gated outfall lets no water into the pipe.
How a LOCAL node's head is advanced turned out to matter more than anything else in the branch. A manhole on a pipe is a weight on a spring. Water in the pipe accelerates toward the lower head, overshoots, and comes back. The second draft moved the node with the head it had at the start of each substep: the face fluxes were fixed from the old head, and those fluxes then moved the head. That is forward Euler on an oscillator, and forward Euler adds a little energy every cycle (Figure 7).
In the resonator test, a dead-end manhole on a surcharged 300-ft pipe started 0.05 ft high, and the draft grew it to a ±2.1 ft limit cycle (FVL-2). Mass was exact the whole time, so the continuity report could not see anything wrong. The lake-at-rest gate caught it. The code was:
fvlink.c, second draft, explicit node coupling (FVL-2)
        for (i = 0; i < NNodes; i++)
        {
            n = NodeList[i];
            NdH[n] = nodeHead(n, t, dt);
...
            NdV[f->n1] -= f->fm[0] * f->barrels * dts;
            NdV[f->n2] += f->fm[nc] * f->barrels * dts;
The fix looks ahead. For each substep the link estimates the node's new head by backward Euler, using the end faces' conductance, √(g·A·T), as the node's dQ/dH, and then re-solves those faces at that head. Up to four estimates are allowed per substep. A node stability limit keeps the substep below the node's area divided by that conductance, A/K. Turn that limit off and the user2 oscillation comes back: user2's largest node depth difference from stock rose from 1.31 ft to 7.05 ft. So the limit stays. With it, the resonator's disturbance falls about 4.6 times in every half hour until the output file can no longer resolve it (Figure 8).
No substep is allowed below 0.001 s. If a stability limit ever asks for less, the substep is raised to the floor and the report counts it as a floor hit, so you know. In the final build no test or sweep model hit the floor. Getting that count right took its own fix: FVL-13 was a substep cut after the fourth estimate that went unrecorded, 18 times in 17.9 million substeps.
Booking the water
Stock SWMM updates a node's volume with the trapezoid rule: half the old flow plus half the new flow, times the step. For an FV link that would be wrong, because the flow through the end face during a routing step is not a straight line between its two end values; it is whatever a hundred substeps made it. So the link books the actual volume that crossed each end face, substep by substep, into the node's continuity (Figure 9). The node's other links keep the trapezoid. The one exception is a node surcharged under EXTRAN, where stock sets the head from the net flow instead of a volume, so the booking cannot be exact there.
The flow the link reports is the flow it delivers: the time-averaged flow out of its downstream face, or out of its upstream face when the net movement is upstream. That is not a cosmetic choice. Quality routing treats a conduit as one inflow plus a change in storage, and the first version reported a flow that counted the storage twice. One pollutant through two FV links gave a quality continuity error of −38,402 % (FVL-8). With the delivered flow, the same model closes to 0.093 % and every concentration is within 0.1 mg/L of stock.
Two more agreements finish the handshake. The FV links are subcycled inside every trial of the dynamic wave step, each time starting again from the state saved at the start of the step, so a trial that is thrown away throws away the FV work too. And the FV links take no part in dynamic wave's Courant step, which is the whole point.
6. Follow the data
Here is the path a number takes, from your input file to your report (Figure 10). The section is read by input.c, which hands each line to fvlink_readParams. A name that is not a link stops the run with ERROR 209; a cell count that is not a positive whole number stops it with ERROR 211. When the project is complete, fvlink_validate checks each listed link and stops the run with ERROR 116 if it cannot be an FV link. When routing starts, fvlink_init builds the 256-depth tables and the cells. Then, every routing step, dynamic wave solves its own links, skipping the FV ones, calls fvlink_findFlows to subcycle them against the current node heads, and updates each node from its booked volumes. At the end, stats.c writes the new Finite-Volume Link Summary, and the .out file carries each FV link's delivered flow like any other link's.
Stock SWMM 5.2.4 reading a file with an [FV_LINKS] section stops with ERROR 205 and writes no .out. That is deliberate. An old engine fails loudly instead of quietly ignoring the section and giving you a dynamic wave answer you think is something else.
The FV Link Summary follows the Routing Time Step Summary. For each FV link it gives the cell count, the cell length, the substeps per routing step (counting every trial), the most substeps in one solve, the smallest substep, the link's volume balance error, and the floor hits. If SWMM's own area table for the link had to be repaired, because its area fell as depth rose (it happens on some irregular transects, never on a built-in shape), the report says so.
7. Checking the work
A solver is an instrument, and you do not use an instrument you have not calibrated. The checks below are mechanical: byte comparisons, rebuilds, analytic answers, mass balances, interleaved timing and sanitizer runs. None of them is somebody's opinion that the curves look about right.
First, prove it changes nothing
With no [FV_LINKS] section, the patched engine was run against stock 5.2.4 on all 73 models of EPA's regression suite. 72 wrote byte-identical .out files. The 73rd stops with the same error in both, because it reads a rain file the suite does not ship. The same FV run made twice writes identical bytes. The patch applied to a fresh clone of the v5.2.4 tag rebuilds a byte-identical binary. Under AddressSanitizer and UBSan, 13 models ran clean, and an OpenMP build with two threads wrote the same .out as the serial build on 13 FV models.
Then, the cases with known answers
The lake at rest. A small network filled to 105 ft everywhere, with an outfall fixed at 105 ft, over a sloped bed, a 0.5 ft offset, two barrels and a surcharged pipe. Nothing should move. With every conduit FV, the largest flow anywhere in two hours was 1.2e-11 cfs (Figure 11). With only some conduits FV, the dynamic wave links settle at about 4e-3 cfs, which is dynamic wave's own noise floor: stock reaches the same level from a 1e-7 ft seed.
Normal depth. A 10-ft rectangular channel carrying 60 cfs at n = 0.015 and S = 0.001 has a Manning normal depth of 1.6559 ft. The FV reach settles at 1.6592 ft (+0.20 %) and carries 60.0001 cfs.
The resonator, already shown, decays as it should. The flap gate, a gated outfall 4 ft above the junction, lets no water back in, the same as stock.
Then, the case that started it
Back to user2 (Figure 12). With TW01290 listed as an FV link, it peaks at 449 cfs instead of 1,921, never reverses, and moves almost exactly the same water: the net volume through the link agrees to 0.02 %. The routing continuity error hardly changes (0.285 % to 0.280 %), which tells you something about continuity: by that measure nothing happened.
Why did SWMM's instability index call the stock run stable? It counts turns, sign changes in a link's step-to-step change in flow, not their size, and lists a link only when the count is high enough. user2 runs 36 hours at 5-s steps, about 25,900 steps, so a link needs roughly 173 turns to appear at all. An oscillation with a period of minutes makes a few dozen. Stock's TW01290 had 45. The FV run has 449 small wiggles in its delivered flow and gets listed with an index of 3, which is the index working as written, not a sign of trouble. If you want to know whether a link is sloshing, look at its total variation, the sum of the sizes of the changes: 38,260 cfs for stock against 965 for FV.
Then, the price at the joints
Here is a cost you should know about before you use it. The node just upstream of an FV link peaks a little higher than in stock (Figure 13). In the 30 cfs chain the excess is 0.41 ft with one cell, 0.19 ft with the default twelve, and 0.13 ft with 48. It shrinks as the cells get shorter, so it is numerical, not a model of entrance loss. The likely causes are the half-cell step in the bed where the pipe meets the node, which OpenSWMM's hydraulics reference describes and cures the same way, with more cells, and the dissipation of the Riemann solver at the end faces. How much is which was not measured.
Then, what it buys
Back to the tree. Seven interleaved runs each, medians: stock with CT21 takes 4.783 s; with CT21 as an FV link it takes 0.896 s (Figure 14). That is 0.19× the wall time, with every interleaved pair between 0.16 and 0.19. The same tree without the short pipe takes 0.580 s in stock, so the FV link itself costs about 1.4× on this network; that comparison is between two different networks, so read it as the price of the link, not a like-for-like test.
And the answer barely moves. Every one of the 400 conduits' peak flows is within 0.53 % of stock, and every node's peak depth within 0.80 % (Figure 15).
Then, everybody else's models
The sweep took each of the 37 dynamic wave models in EPA's suite that has conduits, flagged the conduit with the largest stock peak flow that the validator accepts, and ran it both ways. The flagged conduit's peak moved by a median of 0.04 % (Figure 16). Four moved more than 5 %: user2 (−73 %) and user5 (−38 %), both oscillations; gate_control_2 (+23 %), a gate-release surge that the FV link carries with a sharper front and the same volume; and gate_control_3 (−13 %), a single spike in one 60-s report. The system outflow volume changed by a median of 0.014 %. One model, extran8a, moved 22.7 %, and that traced to stock SWMM, not the branch: it starts two links with an initial flow, and stock recomputes each link's volume from its end depths in the first step. In stock the two jumps cancel; with one link FV the other's stands. It is logged as S5-DW1.
Then, somebody who had not seen it built
A second agent that had not watched the work read the code cold and wrote its own probe models. It found five defects: pumps at an FV end node read the wrong inflow, a flap-gated outfall let water back up the pipe, quality routing counted storage twice, a long link ID overflowed the report line, and the node limiter ignored the node's other outflows. Two more agents checked the written description against the code and the results, and each exposed one more defect. All fourteen are in the defect register, each with the code as it stood when it failed (Figure 17). They are kept because each one is a trap for the next person who writes a scheme like this.
And the engines in this browser
The engines this app runs are not the binaries that were tested above. They are the same source compiled a second time, to WebAssembly, with Emscripten 3.1.51 and LLVM 18, and a second instrument has to be calibrated against the first. Every test, gate and probe model, and all 73 EPA models, were run both ways (Figure 18). Inside the browser the null effect holds exactly: the stock and patched WebAssembly engines write identical bytes on all 73 EPA models. Against the native builds, most runs are byte-identical too. Where they are not, usually only the report differs, in the last digit of a 1e-13 % volume balance or the minute at which a flat peak is reported. The .out values differ on 2 of the 67 test-set runs and on 6 of the 73 EPA models (the same 6 for both engines). The largest absolute difference is 16 cfs in a 1,962-cfs peak, in stock dynamic wave itself on EPA user5 (0.8 %). The largest relative one is 0.44 cfs in a 30-cfs peak (1.5 %), on the reviewer's reversed two-barrel model with every conduit FV. A native Clang build matches the native GCC build on that model, so the compiler is not the cause; the difference follows the math library (musl in the browser build, glibc natively) seeding round-off that a sensitive run amplifies. That was traced by elimination, not proven function by function.
8. What this does not show
Every instrument comes with a specification, and the specification is the list of things it will not do. Here is this one's.
  • No field data. Stock dynamic wave is the reference here, not the truth. When the FV link and stock disagree, nothing in this work says which is closer to the real sewer.
  • Extra head at the joints. The node upstream of an FV link sits higher than in stock, by 0.19 ft at the default mesh in the 30 cfs chain and by 0.47 ft at the storage node in the mixed case. It is numerical and shrinks with refinement. It is not calibrated entrance-loss physics.
  • What an FV link can be (Figure 20). A non-dummy conduit under DYNWAVE routing. Not a force main, not a culvert, not a conduit with a flap gate, any entry, exit or average loss, seepage, a maximum flow, or a street inlet, and not a conduit whose end node feeds a pump or a dummy conduit. Those stop the run with ERROR 116. They are rejected, not supported.
  • What an FV link does not model. Evaporation and seepage inside the link. Water quality was tested with one conservative pollutant only. Hot start files store no cell state, so an FV link restarts at uniform depth.
  • Surcharge. A node surcharged under EXTRAN does not book the FV volume exactly. All 37 EPA sweep models use EXTRAN, and how often their FV end nodes surcharged was not measured.
  • Lengthening. LENGTHENING_STEP does not apply to FV links. In user4, stock lengthens the flagged 1.88-ft link 509-fold; the FV link keeps its true length.
  • Cost (Figure 19). Very short cells and full pipes are expensive. user4's 1.88-ft link has 0.47-ft cells and fast shallow flow: 791 substeps per step, 15.5 s against stock's 3.0 s. A full pipe subcycles at the slot's 100 ft/s whatever its length: extran10's 1,000-ft pipe, under fixed 60-s routing steps, took 957 substeps per step. Use fewer cells on short links, and don't flag a pipe that runs full for hours unless you mean to pay for it.
  • A mixed model at rest sits at dynamic wave's noise floor, about 4e-3 cfs, not at zero.
  • Not tested: reactive pollutants, ponding, hot-start continuity, control rules acting on an FV link, and egg, horseshoe, gothic or custom conduits in a running model (those shapes are covered only by the geometry closure test).
  • Not compared against OpenSWMM's own finite-volume engine.
  • Two platforms. Native Linux with GCC 13.3, serial and OpenMP, and the WebAssembly build in this app. No Windows or MSVC build.
  • This app shows single runs, and browser timing is noisy. Treat its wall-time ratio as a quick look; the 0.19× above comes from interleaved runs on one machine.
9. How to use it
In this app
  1. On the Run tab, pick a sample, or open your own .inp (add any rain or inflow files it reads, in the same picker).
  2. Click a conduit on the network, or tick it in the conduit table, to list it as an FV link. Leave Cells blank for the default (about 25 ft per cell, at least 4). The pre-check marks conduits the engine will reject and says why; the engine has the final word.
  3. Press Run both. The app runs stock 5.2.4 on your model without the FV section, then the patched engine with it, one after the other in a background worker.
  4. Read the cards (wall time, average routing step, continuity), the FV Link Summary, and the peak table. Pick any link or node to compare its hydrograph.
  5. Press Null check to run the patched engine with no FV links and compare its .out with stock's, byte by byte, on your own model.
  6. Export the FV model as .inp, either engine's .rpt and .out, or the comparison tables as CSV.
In an input file
the [FV_LINKS] section
[OPTIONS]
FLOW_ROUTING   DYNWAVE

[FV_LINKS]
;;Link        Cells
C4                     ; default mesh: about 25 ft cells, at least 4
TW01290       40       ; 40 cells
C3            *        ; * = default
Build the native engine from the patch with git apply swmm524-fvlink.patch on a clone of the v5.2.4 tag, then gcc -O2 -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=0 -Isrc/solver -Isrc/solver/include src/solver/*.c src/run/*.c -lm. The package's README, VERIFICATION and DEFECTS files hold the full record.
10. AI use
This branch, its tests, this app and this essay were made with Claude, Anthropic's AI model, in Claude Code sessions from October 13 to 21, 2026, under the direction of Robert (Bob) Dickinson. He asked for finite volume on chosen links with dynamic wave on the rest, for the technical description and the essays, and for this app; responsibility for the work is his.
What Claude did. It read the EPA SWMM 5.2.4 and OpenSWMM source, designed the method and chose its parameters, wrote fvlink.c, the hooks, the test networks and the scripts, ran every test, and fixed the defects in the register. For this app it compiled both engines to WebAssembly, wrote the app (its input, report and output parsers, the network view, the charts and the worker), drew every figure from the results files, and wrote this essay and its Word version. A second Claude agent reviewed the code without the build history, and two more checked drafts of the technical description against the code.
How it was checked. The checks are mechanical: byte comparison with stock on EPA's 73 regression models, rebuilds from the patch, analytic answers, mass balances, interleaved timing, sanitizer runs, the WebAssembly-against-native census, and a headless browser test of this app. What no person has checked yet: fvlink.c line by line, a run on a project model, the design choices listed in the README, and this app's parsers beyond its automated tests.
